items.summary: Following public debate over slowing AI progress—sparked by claims that the technology poses existential risks and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's plan to 'pace the frontier,' which called for common safety standards and limits on unchecked advancement—OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published a blog post proposing perplexity as a shared measurement of AI capability. Perplexity measures how well a model predicts its next token, with lower values indicating better predictions; unlike downstream-capability benchmarks that have become outdated as models advance, Pachocki argues it has remained informative across development. His analysis notes GPT-4's perplexity was approximately 0.91 when the model demonstrated productive chain-of-thought reasoning, and that losses below 0.8 corresponded to emergent capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics. Framing this as a potential 'shared benchmark for general intelligence,' Pachocki suggested companies could commit not to exceed a certain threshold until their ability to understand and monitor AI behavior reaches a concrete milestone; the post was described by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as among the most important things OpenAI has published recently.
items.title: OpenAI's chief scientist proposes perplexity as a benchmark for pacing frontier AI development

items.summary: Consumer products maker Procter & Gamble announced on Nov 19 that it intends to expand the number of factories capable of running shifts without human intervention over the next several years, citing productivity gains and cost savings. The Cincinnati-based company currently operates **15** such unattended sites worldwide and plans to add more by 2027, having invested in automated lines that can run for hours at a time during overnight shifts. Chief product supply officer Luc Reynaert stated the goal is taking “unattended operations to a whole new level,” noting these facilities will improve manufacturing productivity by up to **20%** over four years and save as much as US$10 billion (S$13 billion). The company has also deployed autonomous robots at loading docks and warehouses, along with driverless truck experiments. P&G’s first unattended shift occurred in 2024 at a Gillette factory in Berlin, which now runs without technicians during the overnight shift while freeing staff for less-repetitive or customer-facing daytime tasks; executives acknowledged this requires leaner teams. The announcement coincided with plans to cut its product-supply workforce—encompassing roughly **65,000 workers** across manufacturing, purchasing, planning, engineering and quality control—from 20% to 30% by 2030. However, the company noted these reductions had already been underway for years as part of a supply-chain program called Supply 3.0.
items.title: Procter & Gamble Plans to Expand Human-Free Factory Shifts to Cut Costs

items.summary: On Sunday, US intelligence chief Jay Clayton stated that the United States is investigating an alleged Chinese spy connected to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Speaking on ABC's This Week, Clayton characterized Nvidia chips as "the jewel... that everybody wants," a characterization reported by The New York Times alongside findings that China's spy agency has assisted mainland companies in acquiring advanced chips to advance domestic chip development. According to the reporting, this activity reflects intensified scrutiny of Beijing's efforts to obtain American semiconductor technology amid ongoing US export controls. Brookings expert Kyle Chan told Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast that these restrictions have motivated China to pursue replication of "the entire global semiconductor supply chain," a goal he described as unprecedented for any country. The claims rest on Clayton's characterization, the New York Times reporting, and Chan's analysis; no independent verification of the alleged spy or the specific scope of Chinese acquisition efforts is provided in the text.
items.title: US Intelligence Chief Says Washington Is Probing Alleged Chinese Spy Linked to Jensen Huang

items.summary:
On November 22, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed that developers adopt common limits on increasingly powerful models and use perplexity as a shared metric for measuring progress across the industry. The proposal was presented in a blog post at a time of growing concern about AI's rapidly expanding capabilities.

Pachocki defined perplexity as an intelligence metric reflecting how well a model predicts its next token, noting that lower values indicate better predictions. He proposed capability thresholds based on perplexity and other measurements that developers should commit to not crossing until monitoring and safety mechanisms reach what he described as "a certain concrete milestone." Pachocki argued that AI could drive fundamental advances in training methods by 2027, potentially outpacing progress in monitoring and safety.

The proposal advocated for an industry standard specifying a first limit on development along with the milestones required before exceeding it. CEO Sam Altman publicly supported the initiative, calling his essay "the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile" and asserting that such limits would help ensure safety and control.
items.title: OpenAI Chief Scientist Proposes Industry AI Capability Limits Tied to Perplexity Metric

items.summary: Two independent groups reported that they verified an Anthropic mathematician's proof of the nearly 170-year-old Riemann Hypothesis, which concerns how evenly prime numbers are distributed as they extend toward infinity. The verification came after OpenAI released more than 300 mathematical proofs developed with human oversight, prompting comparisons to AI increasingly tackling long-standing problems under skilled human guidance. A Fields Medal winner told Nature that if the proof fully checks out it would represent a historic milestone in mathematics and is likely correct; a math professor described similar work as remarkable and something seen frequently in the future. The report frames these claims as pending full verification rather than established fact.
items.title: Two Groups Verify Claude-Assisted Proof of Riemann Hypothesis

items.summary:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton stated that the U.S. is investigating an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang—a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International—whom he said had a relationship with Nvidia's former chief executive. Attorney General Todd Blanche reportedly directed the investigation into both Ms. Huang and her company, though no further details were provided.

Clayton characterized Nvidia chips as highly sought after by those willing to break the law for access, noting that they represent "the jewel" at the top of demand. He cited existing indictments involving other companies where individuals broke the law specifically to obtain Nvidia chips, explaining this focus on the company's high-end products.

The reporting relies entirely on statements from Clayton and Blanche; no independent confirmation was provided in the source material regarding Ms. Huang's alleged role or her connection to ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
items.title: U.S. Investigating Alleged Chinese Spy Linked to Ex-Nvidia CEO
